text: A company runs two thousand users on local ServiceNow authentication, with every password checked directly against ServiceNow itself. That company already uses Okta as its enterprise identity platform for everything else, and leadership wants two things at once: move ServiceNow onto SSO against that existing Okta tenant, and have MFA enforced for every login. You're asked to plan this and explain it to a non-technical stakeholder who's going to ask why before approving anything.

Leadership needs the real reasons, applied to this specific company, not a protocol lesson. Right now ServiceNow's password rules exist separately from whatever Okta already enforces everywhere else, so moving to SSO means one policy enforced once, at a system they already manage. Two thousand employees currently juggle a ServiceNow-specific login on top of their Okta login, and SSO collapses that into one. But offboarding is the argument that lands: today, removing a departing employee requires a separate step in ServiceNow on top of disabling them at Okta, and at two thousand users that's two thousand chances to forget it. Under SSO, one Okta action is immediately sufficient.

Before any configuration happens, you need three real pieces, all from Okta, not ServiceNow: the entity ID for this company's Okta tenant, the SSO endpoint URL Okta exposes for this integration, and Okta's current signing certificate. This is a genuine cross-team dependency. Someone with Okta admin access has to retrieve these values and hand them over before the Multi-Provider SSO record can even be built. Planning this migration means scheduling that handoff first.

With Okta's metadata in hand, the Multi-Provider SSO record gets built from exactly those three values. Once saved, the familiar flow applies: a user hits ServiceNow, gets redirected to Okta, authenticates there, and Okta sends back a signed assertion ServiceNow validates before logging the user in. Critically, all two thousand sys_user records keep every existing role and group assignment exactly as they are. This migration changes who verifies identity. It changes nothing about authorization.

This is the step most likely to get over-engineered if you forget the core point from the MFA lesson: enforcement belongs at Okta, not inside ServiceNow. Since Okta is already this company's identity chokepoint, the request to enforce MFA is answered by confirming Okta's own policy covers this integration, not by hunting for a native ServiceNow MFA setting that doesn't exist for this purpose. ServiceNow's configuration doesn't change at all to satisfy that requirement.

If leadership then asks for different MFA rules per department, that's a real, legitimate question, but it's an Okta policy question, not a ServiceNow one. Naming that boundary clearly matters more than guessing at a workaround that doesn't exist. That closes out authentication and SSO for this course. Next up, Chapter Four opens with Edge Encryption and Column-Level Encryption, moving from who gets in to how the data itself stays protected once they're inside.
